units.title: 1 Characteristics and classification of living organisms

outcomes.text: Describe movement and respiration as characteristics of living organisms.
Describe sensitivity and growth as characteristics of living organisms.
Describe reproduction, excretion and nutrition as characteristics of living organisms.

Describe the characteristics of living organisms by describing: (a) movement as an action by an organism or part of an organism causing a change of position or place (b) respiration as the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism (c) sensitivity as the ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment (d) growth as a permanent increase in size and dry mass (e) reproduction as the processes that make more of the same kind of organism (f) excretion as the removal of the waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements (g) nutrition as the taking in of materials for energy, growth and development

topics.title: 1.2 Concept and uses of classification systems

outcomes.text: State that organisms are classified into groups by shared features.
Describe a species as a group able to produce fertile offspring.
Describe the binomial system of genus and species names.
Construct and use dichotomous keys.
Explain that classification aims to reflect evolutionary relationships.
Explain that DNA base sequences are used for classification.
Explain that more closely related organisms have more similar DNA base sequences.
State the main features that place animals and plants in their kingdoms.
State the features that place organisms in the five kingdoms: animal, plant, fungus, prokaryote, protoctist.
State the features of vertebrate groups and arthropod groups.
Classify organisms using these features.
State the features of ferns and flowering plants (dicotyledons and monocotyledons) and classify plants.
State the features of viruses: protein coat and genetic material.
Classify organisms using the features identified in 1.3.4 and 1.3.5
Describe and compare plant and animal cell structures.
Describe the structure of a bacterial cell.
Identify the cell structures in diagrams and images.
Describe the functions of the cell structures.
State that new cells are made by division of existing cells.
State the functions of specialised cells: ciliated, root hair, palisade, neurones, red blood cells and gametes.
Describe cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism.
State and use magnification = image size / actual size.
Calculate magnification and specimen size in millimetres.
Convert between millimetres and micrometres.

units.title: 3 Movement into and out of cells

outcomes.text: Describe diffusion as net movement down a concentration gradient due to random movement.
State that the energy for diffusion comes from kinetic energy of molecules and ions.
State that some substances cross the cell membrane by diffusion.
Describe the importance of diffusion of gases and solutes in organisms.
Investigate how surface area, temperature, concentration gradient and distance affect diffusion.
Describe the role of water as a solvent in digestion, excretion and transport.
State that water diffuses through partially permeable membranes by osmosis, including across cell membranes.
Describe osmosis in terms of water potential and a partially permeable membrane.
Investigate osmosis using materials such as dialysis tubing.

Describe osmosis as the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential (dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (concentrated solution), through a partially permeable membrane
Investigate the effect of different solutions on plant tissues.
Explain effects on plant cells using turgid, turgor pressure, plasmolysis and flaccid.
Explain the importance of water potential and osmosis in water uptake and loss.
State that water pressure in cells supports plants.
State that plants are supported by the pressure of water inside the cells pressing outwards on the cell wall
Describe active transport as movement against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.
State that protein carriers move molecules or ions in active transport.
Explain the importance of active transport, including ion uptake by root hairs.
List the chemical elements in carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
State that large molecules are built from small ones: starch, glycogen, cellulose, proteins and fats.
State that large molecules are made from smaller molecules, limited to: (a) starch, glycogen and cellulose from glucose (b) proteins from amino acids (c) fats and oils from fatty acids and glycerol
Describe the iodine, Benedict's, biuret, ethanol emulsion and DCPIP tests.
Describe DNA as a double helix of two strands joined by paired bases (A-T, C-G).
Describe a catalyst as speeding a reaction without being changed.
Describe enzymes as protein biological catalysts in all metabolic reactions.
Describe why enzymes matter for sustaining life.
Describe enzyme action using the complementary shape of the active site.
Explain enzyme action with active site, enzyme-substrate complex, substrate and product.
Explain enzyme specificity from the complementary shape of the active site.
Investigate the effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity, including optimum and denaturation.
Explain the effect of temperature in terms of kinetic energy, collisions and denaturation.
Explain the effect of pH in terms of shape, fit and denaturation.
Describe why enzymes are important in all living organisms in terms of a reaction rate necessary to sustain life
Describe enzyme action with reference to the shape of the active site of an enzyme being complementary to its substrate and the formation of products
Explain the effect of changes in temperature on enzyme activity in terms of kinetic energy, shape and fit, frequency of effective collisions and denaturation
Describe photosynthesis as making carbohydrates from raw materials using light energy.
State the word and balanced equations for photosynthesis.
State that chlorophyll is a green pigment in chloroplasts that transfers light energy to chemical energy.
Outline the use and storage of photosynthesis products: starch, cellulose, glucose, sucrose and nectar.
Explain the importance of nitrate and magnesium ions.
Investigate the need for chlorophyll, light and carbon dioxide using controls.
Investigate how light intensity, carbon dioxide and temperature affect the rate.
Investigate gas exchange of an aquatic plant in light and dark using hydrogencarbonate indicator.
Identify and explain limiting factors of photosynthesis.
State that leaves are large and thin and explain why that suits photosynthesis.
Identify leaf structures: cuticle, epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, guard cells, stomata, air spaces and vascular bundles.
Explain how these structures adapt leaves for photosynthesis.

Identify in diagrams and images the following structures in the leaf of a dicotyledonous plant: chloroplasts, cuticle, guard cells and stomata, upper and lower epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, air spaces, vascular bundles, xylem and phloem
Describe a balanced diet.
State the sources and importance of carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins C and D, calcium, iron, fibre and water.
State the causes of scurvy and rickets.
Identify the organs of the alimentary canal and the associated organs in diagrams.
Describe organ functions: ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion.
Describe physical digestion and why it speeds chemical digestion by increasing surface area.
Identify the types of human teeth.
Describe tooth structure and the function of each type of tooth.
Describe the stomach's role in physical digestion.
Outline bile's role in emulsifying fats.
Outline the role of bile in emulsifying fats and oils to increase the surface area for chemical digestion
Describe chemical digestion as breaking large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones, so they can be absorbed.
Describe amylase, proteases and lipase and where they are made and act.
Describe hydrochloric acid in gastric juice.
Describe starch digestion by amylase and maltase.
Describe protein digestion by pepsin and trypsin.
Explain how bile neutralises stomach contents for enzyme action.

Describe the functions of enzymes as follows: (a) amylase breaks down starch to simple reducing sugars (b) proteases break down protein to amino acids (c) lipase breaks down fats and oils to fatty acids and glycerol
Describe the functions of hydrochloric acid in gastric juice, limited to killing harmful microorganisms in food and providing an acidic pH for optimum enzyme activity
Explain that bile is an alkaline mixture that neutralises the acidic mixture of food and gastric juices entering the duodenum from the stomach, to provide a suitable pH for enzyme action
State that nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
Explain how villi and microvilli increase surface area and describe a villus.
Describe roles of capillaries and lacteals in villi.
State where water is absorbed: small intestine and colon.
State the functions of xylem and phloem.
Identify xylem and phloem in sections of roots, stems and leaves.
Relate xylem vessel structure to function.
Identify root hair cells and state their function and large surface area.
Outline the pathway of water through root, stem and leaf.
Investigate water pathways in a plant using a stain.
State that the large surface area of root hairs increases the uptake of water and mineral ions
Outline the pathway taken by water through the root, stem and leaf as: root hair cells, root cortex cells, xylem, mesophyll cells
Describe transpiration and how water vapour leaves through stomata.
Explain how water loss relates to air spaces, stomata size and number.
Explain how transpiration pull moves water up the xylem.
Investigate how temperature and wind speed affect transpiration.
Explain how temperature, wind speed and humidity affect the rate.
Explain how and why wilting occurs.
Describe translocation of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from sources to sinks.
Describe sources and sinks.
Explain why a plant part can be a source and a sink at different times.
Describe the circulatory system as vessels, a pump and valves giving one-way flow.
Describe the single circulation of a fish and the double circulation of a mammal.
Explain the advantages of double circulation.
Identify the structures of the mammalian heart, including valves.
Explain the relative thickness of ventricle and atrial walls.
Explain the importance of the septum.
Describe how the heart works through muscle contraction and valve action.
State that arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it.
State how heart activity is monitored: ECG, pulse and valve sounds.
Investigate and explain the effect of physical activity on heart rate.
Describe coronary heart disease and its risk factors.
Discuss how diet and exercise reduce the risk.
Describe the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries.
State the functions of capillaries and explain how structure suits function.
Explain how artery and vein structure relates to blood pressure.
Identify the main vessels to and from the heart, lungs and kidney.
Identify the vessels to and from the liver.
List the components of blood.
Identify red and white blood cells in photomicrographs and diagrams.
State the functions of red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma.
Identify lymphocytes and phagocytes and state their functions.
State the roles of clotting: preventing blood loss and pathogen entry.
Describe clotting as the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin mesh.
Describe a pathogen and a transmissible disease.
State how pathogens are transmitted directly and indirectly.
Describe the body's defences: skin, nose hairs, mucus, stomach acid and white blood cells.
Explain how clean water, hygienic food, personal hygiene, waste disposal and sewage treatment control disease.
Describe active immunity as antibody production against a pathogen.
State that each pathogen has specific antigens.
Describe antibodies binding antigens to destroy or mark pathogens, with complementary shapes.
Explain that active immunity comes from infection or vaccination.
Outline the process of vaccination.
Explain how vaccination controls disease spread.
Explain passive immunity as short-term defence from antibodies acquired from another individual.
Explain the importance of breast-feeding for passive immunity.
State that no memory cells are made in passive immunity.
Describe cholera as a bacterial disease spread in contaminated water.
Explain how the cholera toxin causes diarrhoea, dehydration and ion loss.
State that a pathogen is transmitted: (a) by direct contact, including through blood and other body fluids (b) indirectly, including from contaminated surfaces, food, animals and air
State that each pathogen has its own antigens, which have specific shapes

Outline the process of vaccination: (a) weakened pathogens or their antigens are put into the body (b) the antigens stimulate an immune response by lymphocytes which produce antibodies (c) memory cells are produced that give long-term immunity
Explain that passive immunity is a short-term defence against a pathogen by antibodies acquired from another individual, including across the placenta and in breast milk

Explain that the cholera bacterium produces a toxin that causes secretion of chloride ions into the small intestine, causing osmotic movement of water into the gut, causing diarrhoea, dehydration and loss of ions from the blood
Describe features of human gas exchange surfaces.
Identify parts of the breathing system.
Identify internal and external intercostal muscles and state the function of tracheal cartilage.
Explain how ribs, intercostal muscles and diaphragm change thorax volume and pressure for ventilation.
Investigate differences between inspired and expired air using limewater.
Describe and explain the differences in oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Investigate and describe how physical activity affects the rate and depth of breathing.
Explain this link through carbon dioxide in the blood detected by the brain.
Explain how goblet cells, mucus and ciliated cells protect the breathing system.
State the uses of energy in living organisms.
Investigate the effect of temperature on respiration in yeast.

State the uses of energy in living organisms, including: muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, active transport, growth, the passage of nerve impulses and the maintenance of a constant body temperature
Investigate and describe the effect of temperature on respiration in yeast
Describe aerobic respiration as reactions using oxygen to release energy from nutrients.
State the word and balanced equations for aerobic respiration.
Describe anaerobic respiration as releasing energy without oxygen.
State that it releases much less energy per glucose than aerobic respiration.
State the word and balanced equations for anaerobic respiration in yeast.
State the word equation for anaerobic respiration in muscles.
State that lactic acid builds up causing an oxygen debt.
Outline how the oxygen debt is removed after exercise.
Describe anaerobic respiration as the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules to release energy without using oxygen
State that lactic acid builds up in muscles and blood during vigorous exercise causing an oxygen debt

Outline how the oxygen debt is removed after exercise, limited to: (a) continuation of fast heart rate to transport lactic acid in the blood from the muscles to the liver (b) continuation of deeper and faster breathing to supply oxygen for aerobic respiration of lactic acid (c) aerobic respiration of lactic acid in the liver
State that carbon dioxide is excreted by the lungs and that kidneys excrete urea, excess water and ions.
Explain the importance of excretion: toxicity of urea.
Identify the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra.
Identify the cortex and medulla of the kidney.
Outline nephron structure and function: filtration, reabsorption and urine formation.

Outline the structure and function of a nephron and its associated blood vessels, limited to: (a) the role of the glomerulus in the filtration from the blood of water, glucose, urea and ions (b) the role of the nephron in the reabsorption of all of the glucose, some of the ions and most of the water back into the blood (c) the formation of urine containing urea, excess water and excess ions (details of these processes are not required)
Describe the liver's role in assimilating amino acids into proteins.
State that urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids.
Describe deamination.
Describe deamination as the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of amino acids to form urea
State that electrical impulses travel along neurones.
Describe the CNS and PNS.
Describe the nervous system's role in coordination and regulation.
Identify sensory, relay and motor neurones.
Describe a simple reflex arc: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone and effector.
Describe a reflex action as automatic and rapid coordination.
Describe a synapse as a junction between two neurones.
Describe synapse structure with vesicles, neurotransmitter, synaptic gap and receptor proteins.
Describe the events at a synapse.
State that synapses ensure one-way impulse travel.

Describe the mammalian nervous system in terms of: (a) the central nervous system (CNS) consisting of the brain and the spinal cord (b) the peripheral nervous system (PNS) consisting of the nerves outside of the brain and spinal cord
Describe a reflex action as a means of automatically and rapidly integrating and coordinating stimuli with the responses of effectors (muscles and glands)

Describe the events at a synapse as: (a) an impulse stimulates the release of neurotransmitter molecules from vesicles into the synaptic gap (b) the neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across the gap (c) neurotransmitter molecules bind with receptor proteins on the next neurone (d) an impulse is then stimulated in the next neurone
Describe sense organs as groups of receptor cells responding to specific stimuli.
Identify the structures of the eye, including the blind spot.
Describe the function of cornea, iris, lens, retina and optic nerve.
Describe sense organs as groups of receptor cells responding to specific stimuli: light, sound, touch, temperature and chemicals
Explain the pupil reflex to changes in light intensity.
Explain the pupil reflex through antagonistic circular and radial iris muscles.
Explain accommodation for near and distant objects.
Explain the pupil reflex, limited to changes in light intensity and pupil diameter
Describe the distribution of rods and cones in the retina.
Outline rods for night vision and three cone types for colour vision.
Identify the fovea and state its function.
Describe a hormone as a chemical made by a gland, carried by blood, that alters specific target organs.
Identify the adrenal glands, pancreas, testes and ovaries and the hormones they secrete.
State that glucagon is secreted by the pancreas.
Describe adrenaline in fight or flight, with higher breathing rate, heart rate and pupil diameter.
Describe adrenaline's role in raising blood glucose and heart rate.
Compare nervous and hormonal control by speed and duration.
Describe homeostasis as maintaining a constant internal environment.
Explain negative feedback around a set point.
State that insulin decreases blood glucose.
Describe blood glucose control by the liver, insulin and glucagon.
Outline the treatment of Type 1 diabetes.
Identify structures in the skin.
Describe temperature control by insulation, sweating, shivering and the brain.
Describe temperature control by vasodilation and vasoconstriction.
Identify in diagrams and images of the skin: hairs, hair erector muscles, sweat glands, receptors, sensory neurones, blood vessels and fatty tissue
Describe the maintenance of a constant internal body temperature in mammals in terms of vasodilation and vasoconstriction of arterioles supplying skin surface capillaries
Describe gravitropism.
Describe phototropism.
Investigate gravitropism and phototropism in shoots and roots.
Explain tropisms as chemical control of plant growth.
Explain auxin's role: made in the shoot tip, diffuses, unevenly distributed and stimulates cell elongation.
Describe a drug as a substance that modifies chemical reactions in the body.
Describe antibiotics for treating bacterial infections.
State that antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses.
Describe a drug as any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
State that some bacteria resist antibiotics, reducing their effectiveness.
Explain how using antibiotics only when essential limits resistance such as MRSA.
Describe asexual reproduction as one parent making genetically identical offspring.
Identify examples of asexual reproduction.
Discuss its advantages and disadvantages in wild populations and crops.
Describe sexual reproduction as fusion of two gametes giving genetically different offspring.
Describe fertilisation as fusion of gamete nuclei.
State that gamete nuclei are haploid and the zygote nucleus is diploid.
Discuss its advantages and disadvantages in wild populations and crops.
Identify and draw the parts of an insect-pollinated flower.
State the functions of these parts.
Describe the anthers and stigmas of a wind-pollinated flower and compare the pollen grains.
Describe the structural adaptations of insect- and wind-pollinated flowers.
Describe pollination as transfer of pollen from anther to stigma.
Describe self-pollination and cross-pollination.
Discuss their effects on variation, adaptability and reliance on pollinators.
State that fertilisation is fusion of a pollen nucleus with an ovule nucleus.
Describe pollen tube growth into the ovule before fertilisation.
Investigate how water, oxygen and temperature affect germination.
Identify the male reproductive organs and state their functions.
Identify the female reproductive organs and state their functions.
Describe fertilisation as fusion of sperm and egg nuclei.
Explain adaptive features of sperm.
Explain adaptive features of egg cells.
Compare male and female gametes in size, structure, motility and numbers.
State that the zygote forms an embryo that implants in the uterus lining.
Identify the umbilical cord, placenta, amniotic sac and fluid and state their functions.
Describe how the placenta and cord exchange nutrients, gases and wastes between mother and fetus.
State that some pathogens and toxins cross the placenta.
State that in early development, the zygote forms an embryo which is a ball of cells that implants into the lining of the uterus
State that some pathogens and toxins can pass across the placenta and affect the fetus
Describe the roles of testosterone and oestrogen at puberty.
Describe the menstrual cycle through ovary and uterus lining changes.
Describe where oestrogen and progesterone are produced in the cycle and pregnancy.
Explain hormone control of the cycle and pregnancy: FSH, LH, progesterone, oestrogen.
Describe an STI as an infection spread by sexual contact.
State that HIV is an STI pathogen and may lead to AIDS.
Describe how HIV is transmitted.
Explain how the spread of STIs is controlled.
State that chromosomes are made of DNA containing genes.
Define a gene as a length of DNA coding for a protein.
Define an allele.
Describe the inheritance of sex with X and Y chromosomes.
State that the base sequence in a gene determines the amino acid sequence.
Explain that amino acid sequences give proteins different shapes.
Explain that DNA controls cell function by controlling protein production.
Explain how a protein is made using mRNA and ribosomes.
Explain that most cells hold the same genes but express only some.
Describe haploid and diploid nuclei.
State that diploid cells have chromosome pairs, 23 in humans.
State that chromosomes are made of DNA, which contains genetic information in the form of genes
Define an allele as an alternative form of a gene
Explain that DNA controls cell function by controlling the production of proteins, including enzymes, membrane carriers and receptors for neurotransmitters

Explain how a protein is made, limited to: • the gene coding for the protein remains in the nucleus • messenger RNA (mRNA) is a copy of a gene • mRNA molecules are made in the nucleus and move to the cytoplasm • the mRNA passes through ribosomes • the ribosome assembles amino acids into protein molecules • the specific sequence of amino acids is determined by the sequence of bases in the mRNA (knowledge of the details of transcription or translation is not required)
Explain that most body cells in an organism contain the same genes, but many genes in a particular cell are not expressed because the cell only makes the specific proteins it needs
Describe mitosis as nuclear division giving genetically identical cells.
State the roles of mitosis in growth, repair, replacement and asexual reproduction.
State that chromosomes replicate before mitosis and the copies separate.
Describe stem cells.
State that the exact replication of chromosomes occurs before mitosis
State that during mitosis, the copies of chromosomes separate, maintaining the chromosome number in each daughter cell
Describe stem cells as unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised for specific functions
State that meiosis produces gametes.
Describe meiosis as reduction division from diploid to haploid giving genetically different cells.
Describe inheritance as transmission of genetic information between generations.
Describe genotype and phenotype.
Describe homozygous and heterozygous, and pure-breeding.
Describe dominant and recessive alleles.
Interpret pedigree diagrams.
Use genetic diagrams for monohybrid crosses and 1:1 and 3:1 ratios.
Use Punnett squares to show possible genotypes.
Explain how a test cross identifies an unknown genotype.
Describe codominance.
Explain inheritance of ABO blood groups.
Describe sex-linked characteristics and red-green colour blindness.
Use genetic diagrams for crosses involving codominance or sex linkage.
Describe variation as differences between individuals of a species.
State continuous variation and give examples.
State discontinuous variation and give examples.
State that discontinuous variation is caused by genes, and continuous by genes and environment.
Investigate examples of continuous and discontinuous variation.
Describe mutation as genetic change and gene mutation as a random base sequence change.
State that mutation forms new alleles.
State that ionising radiation and some chemicals raise the mutation rate.
State that mutation, meiosis, random mating and random fertilisation cause variation.
State that continuous variation results in a range of phenotypes between two extremes; examples include body length and body mass
State that discontinuous variation results in a limited number of phenotypes with no intermediates; examples include ABO blood groups, seed shape in peas and seed colour in peas
State that discontinuous variation is usually caused by genes only and continuous variation is caused by both genes and the environment
State that mutation, meiosis, random mating and random fertilisation are sources of genetic variation in populations
Describe an adaptive feature as an inherited feature that helps survival and reproduction.
Interpret information about a species to describe its adaptive features.
Explain adaptive features of hydrophytes and xerophytes.
Describe natural selection: variation, many offspring, struggle for survival, better-adapted individuals reproducing and passing on alleles.
Describe adaptation as populations becoming better suited over generations.
Describe the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria as natural selection.
Describe selective breeding: choose, cross and select offspring with desirable features.
Outline how selective breeding improves crops and animals over many generations.
Outline the differences between natural and artificial selection.
State that the Sun is the main energy source for biological systems.
Describe energy flow through organisms and its eventual transfer to the environment.
Describe a food chain, starting with a producer.
Construct and interpret simple food chains.
Describe and interpret food webs.
Describe a food chain as showing the transfer of energy from one organism to the next, beginning with a producer
Describe producers and consumers.
State primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary consumers.
Describe herbivores, carnivores and decomposers.
Use food chains and webs to describe overharvesting and introduced species.
Draw, describe and interpret pyramids of numbers and biomass.
Discuss pyramid of biomass versus numbers.
Draw, describe and interpret pyramids of energy.
Discuss pyramids of energy versus numbers or biomass.
Describe trophic levels and identify them in webs, chains and pyramids.
Explain why energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient.
Explain why food chains rarely have over five trophic levels.
Explain why eating crop plants is more energy efficient than eating livestock.
Describe the carbon cycle.
Describe the nitrogen cycle steps.
State the roles of microorganisms in the nitrogen cycle.
Describe a population, a community and an ecosystem.
Identify factors affecting population growth: food, competition, predation, disease.
Identify lag, exponential, stationary and death phases of the sigmoid growth curve.
Explain the factors behind each phase, including limiting factors.
Interpret graphs and diagrams of population growth.
Describe how machinery, fertilisers, insecticides, herbicides and selective breeding increase food production.
Describe the advantages and disadvantages of large-scale monocultures.
Describe the advantages and disadvantages of intensive livestock production.
Describe biodiversity.
Describe reasons for habitat destruction: housing and farmland, resource extraction and pollution.
State that altering food webs and chains harms habitats.
Describe biodiversity as the number of different species that live in an area

Describe the reasons for habitat destruction, including: (a) increased area for housing, crop plant production and livestock production (b) extraction of natural resources (c) freshwater and marine pollution
Explain the effects of deforestation: lost biodiversity, extinction, soil loss, flooding and more carbon dioxide.
Describe effects of untreated sewage and excess fertiliser on aquatic ecosystems.
Explain eutrophication.
Describe effects of non-biodegradable plastics.
Describe sources and effects of methane and carbon dioxide pollution: enhanced greenhouse effect and climate change.
Describe the effects of non-biodegradable plastics, in both aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems
Describe a sustainable resource.
State that forests and fish stocks can be conserved and managed sustainably.
Explain how forests are conserved.
Explain how fish stocks are conserved.
Explain why organisms become endangered or extinct.
Describe how endangered species are conserved.
Describe reasons for conservation programmes.
Describe artificial insemination and IVF in captive breeding.
Explain the risks of reduced genetic variation when a population shrinks.
State that bacteria are useful because they reproduce quickly and make complex molecules.
Discuss why bacteria are useful: few ethical concerns and the presence of plasmids.
Describe anaerobic respiration in yeast for ethanol biofuels.
Describe anaerobic respiration in yeast in bread-making.
Describe pectinase in fruit juice production.
Investigate biological washing powders containing enzymes.
Explain lactase use to make lactose-free milk.
Describe how fermenters produce insulin, penicillin and mycoprotein.
Describe and explain conditions controlled in a fermenter.
Describe genetic modification as removing, changing or inserting genes.
Outline the process using bacterial production of a human protein.
Outline examples: human proteins in bacteria and herbicide resistance, insect resistance and better nutrition in crops.
Discuss advantages and disadvantages of genetically modified crops such as soya, maize and rice.
